flawed_step: Step 1: If a vertex receives greedy color k, it has previously colored neighbors of every color 1,...,k-1; justified. Step 2: To obtain k <= chi(G)+1, one would infer that these differently colored neighbors force chi(G) >= k-1. This is unjustified: those neighbors need not be pairwise adjacent, and greedy color labels do not yield a chromatic-number lower bound.
counterexample: Let G have vertices a,b1,b2,c1,c2,c3,c4,r and edges {r-a, r-b2, r-c4, b1-b2, c2-c3, c4-c1, c4-c3}. This is a tree, with bipartition {r,b1,c1,c3} and {a,b2,c2,c4}; since it has edges, chi(G)=2. Process vertices in the order a,b1,b2,c1,c2,c3,c4,r. Greedy colors are: a=1; b1=1; b2=2 (sees b1); c1=1; c2=1; c3=2 (sees c2); c4=3 (sees c1 with color 1 and c3 with color 2); r=4 (sees a,b2,c4 with colors 1,2,3). Thus greedy uses 4 colors, but chi(G)+1=3.
assessment_summary: The proposed bound is false. A specific 8-vertex tree and processing order make greedy coloring use four colors although the graph has chromatic number two.
